design_detail: Anonymous cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics), January to December 2017, of adults (18 or over, English-proficient) who had used kratom in the past year, recruited by online advertisements and email announcements on sites of interest to people who use kratom (the American Kratom Association, Erowid and Reddit are given as examples); 53% of the final sample learned of it through the American Kratom Association. 4,302 began, 2,826 (66%) met all criteria and completed, and 28 were removed for inconsistent responses or technical problems, leaving 2,798. Measures: demographics, past-year substance use, lifetime diagnoses, PROMIS Global Health, Brief Pain Inventory, kratom use patterns, reasons for use with 0–100 effectiveness ratings, whether kratom had been used to cut down or stop opioids, adverse effects, possible kratom withdrawal (Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale for those endorsing it), 13 Drug Effects Questionnaire items, a 0–100 rating of being troubled by kratom use, and a DSM-5 substance use disorder symptom checklist for past-year kratom use. Descriptive statistics; chi-square and Mann-Whitney tests comparing respondents who had used kratom to reduce opioid use (n=1,144) with the others (n=1,654); four multivariable logistic regressions (adverse effects, withdrawal, treatment-seeking, use to reduce opioids). Read as the online-first corrected proof (Article in Press).
can_establish: What 2,798 self-selected adults who had used kratom in the past year, reached mostly through a kratom advocacy organization and social media in 2017, reported about their health, how and why they used kratom, how effective they rated it, whether they had used it to cut down or stop opioids, adverse and withdrawal effects and DSM-5 use-disorder symptoms, and how those who had used it to reduce opioids differed from the others.
cannot_establish: How common these patterns, benefits or harms are among people who use kratom (no sampling frame; recruitment through advocacy and enthusiast sites; people who stopped because of harm may be under-represented, as the authors say); whether kratom helps people stop opioids or relieves pain or mood symptoms (self-attributed, retrospective, no comparison group, opioid abstinence not verified); or whether kratom carries less risk than opioids (no opioid comparison).

sample.recruitment: Online advertisements and email announcements on sites of interest to people who use kratom (American Kratom Association, Erowid and Reddit as examples); 53% of the final sample learned of the survey through the American Kratom Association and 44.2% through Facebook or other social media (p. 2, 2.1; p. 3, 3.1). No incentive, except $3.10 for each of 36 pilot respondents recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk; whether they are in the final sample is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 or over, English proficiency, kratom use in the past year; consent by choosing to begin; IP addresses collected to prevent repeat responses and destroyed after collection; the institutional review board judged the study not to be human subjects research (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Mean age 40.2 (SD 11.8); 60.7% women; White 89.8%; 66.5% married or in a committed relationship; 68.4% employed, 11.2% unemployed; 83.9% at least some college; US South 41.0%, outside the US or not stated 2.9% (Table 1, p. 3). Past-year use: alcohol 47.4%, tobacco 42.2%, cannabis 37.2%, opioids prescribed or illicit 33.0%, antidepressants 28.1%, benzodiazepines 25.1%. Chronic pain in the past 3 months 68.8%; lifetime back pain 72.5%, depression 65.0%, panic attacks 48.1%, PTSD 25.4% (pp. 3–4).
sample.attrition: Single survey. 1,476 of the 4,302 who began (34%) did not complete or did not meet the criteria and are not described (editors' calculation).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected convenience sample recruited through advocacy and enthusiast websites; the authors say it is likely biased toward younger, more affluent people positively inclined toward kratom and may under-represent people of lower socio-economic status, older and less technologically fluent people, and people with negative experiences who stopped, so adverse effects may be underestimated and benefits overestimated (pp. 6–7). 80.7% had used kratom in the 24 hours before the survey and 59.1% used it daily, so the sample is weighted toward current, regular use.

exposure.measurement: Self-report; neither kratom use nor the product was verified.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, as study conditions (Table 2, p. 5): typical amount per occasion under 1 g 8.6%, 1–3 g 49.0%, 4–6 g 33.4%, 7 g or more 8.9%; mean 2.7 (SD 1.3) doses a day; past-year frequency daily 59.1%, 4–6 times a week 18.2%, 2–3 times a week 13.4%, 2–4 times a month 5.4%, once a month or less 3.9%; route: powder swallowed 43.6%, tea or other beverage 37.0%, capsules or pills 18.9%, other (for example smoked, intravenous or subcutaneous, extract) 0.4%; used 100 or more times 76.2%; mean age at first use 38.0 (SD 12.2).
exposure.polysubstance: Past-year use of other substances recorded (Table 1); past-year alcohol and opioid use, and the number of opioid types used, entered as predictors in the regressions; not otherwise handled. 52.9% had ever experienced opioid withdrawal or difficulty controlling opioid use (p. 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; 80.7% had used kratom in the 24 hours before completing the survey.

comparison.controls: Internal comparison: respondents who answered yes to having ever used kratom to cut down or stop heroin or prescription pain medications (n=1,144) against the other respondents (n=1,654), with chi-square and two-tailed Mann-Whitney tests (Tables 1 and 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity of opioid use and of any opioid use disorder before kratom; treatment history (past-year buprenorphine-naloxone and methadone were asked only of the opioid-reduction group); access to medical care, which the authors say was not probed (p. 6); kratom product type.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group also used other substances in the past year: opioids 22.5%, benzodiazepines 22.7%, alcohol 50.7% (Table 1, p. 3).

outcomes.instruments: PROMIS Global Health (10 items); Brief Pain Inventory (15 items); Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (16 items, 0–64; completed only by respondents endorsing possible kratom withdrawal); Drug Effects Questionnaire (13 items on 0–100 visual analogue scales); a 0–100 scale of being troubled or bothered by kratom use; a DSM-5 substance use disorder symptom checklist for past-year kratom use; study-specific items on reasons for use, effectiveness (0–100), recommending kratom, use to reduce opioids, and adverse effects with severity, duration and medical treatment (p. 2, 2.2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments for health, pain, opioid withdrawal and subjective effects, used online and self-completed; the DSM-5 checklist was self-completed, not a clinical interview. Opioid abstinence was self-reported and its attribution to kratom was the respondent's.
outcomes.operationalization: Adverse effects: yes, maybe or no to any adverse or side effect attributed to kratom. Withdrawal: yes, maybe or no to kratom-related withdrawal symptoms. Use disorder: DSM-5 criteria from the checklist, grouped as none, mild, moderate or severe. Opioid reduction: yes to the question on ever using kratom to cut down or stop heroin or prescription pain medications (Table 1 footnote a).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: about 66 between-group tests in Tables 1 and 2 (editors' count) and four logistic regressions with many predictors each, reported only where significant.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages and means (Tables 1 and 2): reasons for use pain 91.3%, anxiety 67.2%, depression 64.5%; effectiveness ratings 83.3 (pain), 76.7 (anxiety), 76.5 (depression) on 0–100; used kratom to cut down or stop opioids 1,144 (40.9%), of whom 849 (74.2%) reported at least 6 months of abstinence attributed to kratom; adverse effects yes 19.3%, maybe 12.8%; sought medical treatment 17 (0.6%); kratom withdrawal yes 9.5%, maybe 17.5%; DSM-5 checklist mild 9.9%, moderate 1.8%, severe 0.6%; troubled by kratom use 3.2 (SD 9.8) on 0–100. Logistic regressions (adjusted odds ratios, 95% CI): withdrawal and female sex 0.21 (0.09–0.47), never having had opioid withdrawal 0.14 (0.05–0.36); adverse effects and female sex 0.75 (0.59–0.95), no past-year alcohol 0.61 (0.48–0.76), no past-year opioids 0.59 (0.45–0.76), no depression 0.68 (0.54–0.87); use to reduce opioids and past-year opioid use 5.89 (3.35–10.39), fewer than 100 lifetime uses of kratom 0.26 (0.13–0.52). Other regression results are given as bounds with min-to-max ranges (see reporting issues). Editors' calculation: moderate or severe use disorder 68 of 2,798 (2.4%, Wilson 95% interval 1.9% to 3.1%); sought treatment 17 of 2,798 (Wilson 0.4% to 1.0%).
analysis.covariates: Regression predictors: age, sex, race, relationship status, education, employment, income, region, past-year alcohol and opioid use, bipolar disorder, depression, age at first kratom use, frequency of kratom use, number of use-disorder symptoms, SOWS total, pain severity, ever having had opioid withdrawal, and the number of opioid types used in the past year (pp. 2–3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Regression results are given only for significant predictors, as bounds (for example greater than 1.20) with, per footnote 1, the range from minimum to maximum across categories in place of intervals; non-significant predictors and the numbers in each model are not reported. The number completing the SOWS is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported. The sample is large for headline shares (about ±1.9 percentage points near 50%, editors' calculation), but regression intervals reaching 1.21 × 10^10 and 1.44 × 10^13 indicate sparse categories.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2,798 self-selected adults who had used kratom in the past year, surveyed online in 2017 (53% reached through the American Kratom Association), most used it daily (59.1%), mainly for pain (91.3%), anxiety (67.2%) and depression (64.5%), and rated it highly. 1,144 (40.9%) had used it to cut down or stop opioids, and 849 of them reported at least 6 months without opioids that they attributed to kratom. Adverse effects were reported by 19.3% and possible adverse effects by 12.8%, mostly mild and lasting a day or less; 17 (0.6%) sought medical treatment. Kratom withdrawal was reported by 9.5% (possible 17.5%); on the DSM-5 checklist 9.9% met criteria for mild and 68 (2.4%) for moderate or severe use disorder (editors' calculation). Those who had used kratom to reduce opioids used it more often and in larger amounts, and more often reported withdrawal.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives 56 (2%) with moderate or severe use disorder where Table 2 gives 68 (2.4%), and says 411 reported more than 1 year of continuous abstinence from opioids attributed to kratom, a description the Results give to no figure (p. 1 against pp. 4–5). The conclusion that kratom-related use disorder and serious adverse effects were uncommon (p. 1) describes this sample, which the authors say may under-represent people with negative experiences who stopped (p. 7). The Discussion's "relatively benign risk profile compared to typical opioids" (p. 6) rests on no comparison with opioids in the data, and its statements that kratom may have significant therapeutic potential and that banning it would push people back to opioids (pp. 6–7) go beyond a cross-sectional survey of people who continue to use kratom. The Discussion also says the data suggest that individuals in the US are using kratom to self-treat pain, depression, anxiety and opioid withdrawal and reporting robust effectiveness (p. 6), a statement about people in the US drawn from this self-selected sample. Effectiveness ratings are the respondents' own, without comparison or verification. In fairness, the limitations are stated plainly and the paper calls for nationally representative and controlled studies (p. 7). A headline version (kratom helps people quit opioids; kratom addiction is rare) would overstate what self-reports from this sample can show.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: only Grundmann (2017) of the related surveys was read for this card. Online surveys of people who use kratom agree on use for pain, mood and opioid reduction, high perceived effectiveness and few reported serious harms, but all draw on self-selected samples reached through advocacy and enthusiast channels; the paper names a single controlled human study to date and calls for nationally representative and controlled research (p. 7). The project's Kratom list notes that no randomised trials of kratom in humans and no cohort studies of long-term outcomes were found.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies of people using kratom to stop opioids, with opioid abstinence verified by urine testing and compared with people receiving buprenorphine or methadone, and randomized trials; for how common use disorder and harms are, probability-based surveys with clinical interviews of everyone, including people who have stopped using kratom.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: Self-selected convenience sample.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 2,798 respondents: intervals of about ±1.9 percentage points for shares near 50% (editors' calculation); rare outcomes such as treatment-seeking (17) are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics, health, substance use and diagnoses are described in detail (Table 1).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 1,476 of the 4,302 who began (34%) did not complete or did not meet criteria and are not described (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Standard instruments for health, pain, withdrawal (SOWS) and subjective effects, and a DSM-5 checklist, all self-completed online; opioid abstinence and its attribution to kratom are self-reported and unverified.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence for a survey that reports how often patterns, benefits and harms occurred among respondents. Editors' summary: high risk of bias for any figure beyond this sample: an advocacy- and enthusiast-recruited convenience sample weighted toward daily, continuing use, self-reported and unverified outcomes, and an unreliable regression analysis. The direction of bias is toward more benefit and less harm than among everyone who has used kratom, as the authors say. Citable for: what these 2,798 respondents reported in 2017 (reasons, patterns and perceived effectiveness; 40.9% had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids and 849 reported at least 6 months of abstinence they attributed to kratom; adverse effects 19.3%, treatment sought 0.6%; withdrawal 9.5%; DSM-5 checklist 9.9% mild and 68, 2.4%, moderate or severe), labelled as a self-selected sample. Not citable for: how common use disorder or harms are among people who use kratom, kratom's efficacy for opioid withdrawal or abstinence, any comparison with opioids, or regression estimates beyond the few clearly reported.

key_findings.finding: Anonymous online survey, January to December 2017, advertised on sites of interest to people who use kratom (the American Kratom Association, Erowid and Reddit as examples); required age 18 or over, English proficiency and kratom use in the past year. Of 4,302 who began, 2,826 (66%) met all criteria and completed, and 28 were removed for inconsistent responses or technical issues, leaving 2,798; 53% had learned of the survey through the American Kratom Association and 44.2% through Facebook or other social media. No incentive, except $3.10 for each of 36 pilot respondents on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Data collection (one paragraph, p. 2); 3.1 Sample characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Respondents: mean age 40.2 (SD 11.8); 60.7% women; White 89.8%; 66.5% married or in a committed relationship; 68.4% employed; 83.9% with at least some college; 41.0% in the US South. Past-year use: alcohol 47.4%, tobacco 42.2%, cannabis 37.2%, opioids prescribed or illicit 33.0%, antidepressants 28.1%, benzodiazepines 25.1%. 52.9% had ever experienced opioid withdrawal symptoms or difficulty controlling opioid use.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Sample characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: 1,924 (68.8%) reported chronic pain over the past 3 months, with mean Brief Pain Inventory severity 4.1 (SD 1.8) and interference 4.9 (2.9) on 0–10 scales; of them, 39.4% were taking a prescribed pain medication and 87.6% were using kratom for pain. Lifetime diagnoses: back pain 72.5%, depression 65.0%, muscle pain 62.9%, panic attacks 48.1%, arthritis 43.8%, PTSD 25.4%. PROMIS Global Health physical 13.7 (3.2) and mental 12.8 (3.5), which the authors convert to T-scores of about 45 against a US mean of 50.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Physical and psychological health, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Table 1 (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: Use patterns: 76.2% had used kratom 100 or more times and 80.7% in the 24 hours before the survey; daily use 59.1%; mean number of doses per day 2.7 (SD 1.3), which Table 2 gives for the whole sample of 2,798, not only for those using kratom daily (the text places it after the daily-use share); typical amount per occasion 1–3 g for 49.0% and 4–6 g for 33.4% (under 1 g 8.6%, 7 g or more 8.9%); swallowed as powder 43.6%, as a tea or other beverage 37.0%, capsules or pills 18.9%, other routes 12 respondents (0.4%); mean age at first use 38.0 (12.2).
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Reasons for kratom use and use patterns, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Respondents endorsed using kratom for pain relief (91.3%), anxiety (67.2%), depression (64.5%), post-traumatic stress (29.6%) and bipolar mood (24.6%), and the first reasons row of Table 2, treatment of mood-related or psychiatric symptoms, gives 1,975 (70.6%); mean effectiveness ratings on a 0–100 scale were 83.3 (SD 18.5) for pain, 76.7 (24.3) for anxiety, 76.5 (25.4) for depression, 60.2 (38.2) for post-traumatic stress and 51.4 (39.9) for bipolar mood; of those using it for these reasons, 98.7% would recommend kratom for pain relief and 96.7% for mood-related issues.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Reasons for kratom use and use patterns, 1st paragraph (pp. 3–4); Table 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: 1,144 respondents (40.9%) had used kratom to reduce or stop opioid use (prescription opioid medications and heroin). Of them, 87.3% (999) said it effectively treated their opioid withdrawal symptoms, 86.1% (985) that it addressed pain underlying their opioid use, 79.6% (911) that it reduced opioid cravings and 72.0% (824) that it improved mood while tapering; withdrawal symptoms reported as reduced included anxiety (86.5%, 989), body aches (86.5%, 989), restlessness (86.4%, 988) and insomnia (79.5%, 910).
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Kratom for opioid use reduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the opioid-reduction group, past-year opioid use was most often Percocet (33.2%, 380) or Vicodin (32.3%, 369), heroin 5.8% (66); 122 (10.7%) reported past-year Suboxone and 89 (7.8%) methadone use; 411 (35.9%) reported no past-year opioid use; 849 (74.2%) reported at least 6 months of abstinence from opioids that they attributed to kratom; and 1,135 (99.2%) would recommend kratom as an opioid withdrawal treatment.
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Kratom for opioid use reduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Self-reported and retrospective; abstinence was not verified, and prescribed and illicit use of opioid medications could not be distinguished (p. 7). Table 1 gives 550 of the 1,144 with past-12-month opioid use, which does not match 411 without (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 540 (19.3%) reported adverse effects from kratom and 357 (12.8%) possible adverse effects; among those reporting definite or possible adverse effects, 9 (1%) rated them serious to extreme, 47 moderate and 567 mild (63.2%), 772 (86.1%) said they lasted a day or less and 13 a year or more, and 17 (1.9% of them; 0.6% of all 2,798) sought medical treatment. Editors' calculation: the definite or possible group numbers 897.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Kratom adverse effects (one paragraph, p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Kratom-related withdrawal symptoms: yes 267 (9.5%), maybe 491 (17.5%), no 2,040 (72.9%); mean Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale score 8.8 (SD 8.4), in the range the authors call mild (below 11), among those who completed it. DSM-5 checklist for past-year kratom-related use disorder: no criteria met 2,454 (87.7%), mild 276 (9.9%), moderate 51 (1.8%), severe 17 (0.6%). Mean rating of being troubled or bothered by kratom use 3.2 (SD 9.8) on a 0–100 scale. Editors' calculation: moderate or severe 68 (2.4%; Wilson 95% interval 1.9% to 3.1%).
key_findings.locator: 3.4, last sentences, and 3.5 Symptoms of withdrawal following kratom abstinence (one paragraph) (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 56 (2%) for moderate or severe use disorder (see reporting issues). The number completing the SOWS is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Typical kratom effects on 0–100 scales (Drug Effects Questionnaire, all 13 items, in rank order): good effects 86.4 (SD 23.0), drug liking 85.7 (23.7), alert 49.8 (30.9), stimulated 41.3 (28.6), desire 30.1 (28.9), drug effect 27.3 (29.8), euphoric 25.1 (27.1), sleepy 22.3 (23.6), high 12.0 (20.1), bad effects 11.5 (15.7), sick 6.2 (12.3), dizzy 4.8 (10.9), anxious 3.9 (9.6). The Methods give drug liking, euphoria and desire as examples of items associated with abuse liability.
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Measures, 3rd paragraph (p. 2); 3.5 (p. 4); Table 2 (pp. 5–6)

key_findings.finding: Respondents who had used kratom to reduce opioid use (n=1,144) against the others (n=1,654): daily use 69.5% against 51.9%; mean doses a day 3.1 against 2.4; kratom withdrawal yes 12.2% against 7.7%; no use-disorder criteria met 85.8% against 89.1%; past-year opioids 48.1% against 22.5%, tobacco 50.1% against 36.7%, benzodiazepines 28.6% against 22.7%, cocaine 5.0% against 2.8%, alcohol 42.7% against 50.7%; unemployed 12.9% against 10.0%; drug liking 87.3 against 84.6.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 3); Table 2 (p. 5); section 3.7, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: In the logistic regressions, kratom withdrawal was predicted by the number of DSM-5 use-disorder symptoms (χ2 = 3301.90), female sex (aOR 0.21, 95% CI 0.09–0.47), the SOWS total (χ2 = 77.25) and never having experienced opioid withdrawal (aOR 0.14, 0.05–0.36); adverse effects by female sex (0.75, 0.59–0.95), no past-year alcohol (0.61, 0.48–0.76), no past-year opioid use (0.59, 0.45–0.76) and no depression (0.68, 0.54–0.87); use to reduce opioids by past-year opioid use (5.89, 3.35–10.39) and fewer than 100 lifetime kratom uses (0.26, 0.13–0.52).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 and 3.5 (p. 4); 3.6, end of 2nd paragraph (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Several other estimates are printed as bounds with intervals that include 1 or reach 10^10 and 10^13, and two predictors restate the withdrawal outcome (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the main limitation is the self-selected convenience sample: because data were collected online and recruitment ran through websites of interest to people who use kratom, the sample likely exhibits selection bias toward younger, more affluent people more positively inclined toward kratom, so the results may under-represent people of lower socio-economic status, older and less technologically fluent people, and those with negative experiences of kratom (for example, people who stopped because of adverse effects), and adverse effects may be underestimated and benefits overestimated; they add that prescribed and illicit use of opioid medications could not be distinguished.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says fifty-six individuals (2%) met DSM-5 criteria for past-year moderate or severe kratom-related use disorder; Table 2 gives 51 moderate (1.8%) and 17 severe (0.6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table's four rows sum to 2,798 and give 68 (2.4%; editors' calculation); the abstract's 56 is unexplained. Cite 68 of 2,798.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports 411 respondents with more than 1 year of continuous abstinence from opioids attributed to kratom; in the Results, 411 (35.9%) is the number in the opioid-reduction group reporting no past-year opioid use, with nothing on continuity or attribution, and the attribution to kratom is reported for at least 6 months of abstinence (849, 74.2%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's description of the 411 is not supported by the Results; claims should use 849 reporting at least 6 months of abstinence that they attributed to kratom, as self-report.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 shows 550 of the 1,144 in the opioid-reduction group (48.1%) with past-12-month use of opioids, prescribed or illicit, while the Results give 411 (35.9%) with no past-year opioid use; editors' calculation: Table 1 leaves 594 without past-12-month opioid use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two counts of the same group without past-year opioid use disagree (594 against 411), and the question behind each is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: Regression results are printed as bounds with intervals that include 1 although the predictor is called significant (for example aOR greater than 1.20 for age 65 or younger, 95% CI 0.18 to 13.42); footnote 1 says the interval shown is the range from minimum to maximum across categories; some intervals reach 1.21 × 10^10 and 1.44 × 10^13, and the chi-square for pain severity is 9240.28 with 2,798 respondents.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed ranges are not confidence intervals, and several estimates point to sparse categories or separation; only the clearly reported odds ratios (for example female sex and withdrawal, 0.21, 0.09–0.47) should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The withdrawal model includes as predictors the SOWS total, which only respondents endorsing possible withdrawal completed, and the number of DSM-5 use-disorder symptoms, which include withdrawal; the treatment-seeking model uses the same two predictors.
reporting_issues.consequence: These predictors partly restate the outcome, so their strong associations (for example χ2 = 3301.90 for symptom count) and the improved model fit say little about what predicts withdrawal.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 shows the SOWS score (8.8 ± 8.4) in the total-sample column and compares the two groups on it, although the scale was completed only by respondents endorsing possible kratom withdrawal; how many completed it is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mean describes an unstated subset, not the whole sample (editors' calculation: at most the 758 answering yes or maybe).

reporting_issues.issue: The household-income categories in Table 1 leave a gap ($50,000–$62,999 is followed by $70,000–$99,999), the text gives a median of $50,000–$59,000, which is not a table category, and the adverse-effects model refers to earnings under $250k, a category not in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Income was apparently asked in finer categories than shown; the median and the categories cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that respondents who used kratom daily were unlikely to meet criteria for a kratom-related use disorder, but no analysis of use disorder by frequency of use is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot be checked from the paper; the only related figures are for the whole sample and for the two motivation groups (editors' calculation: 344 of 2,798, 12.3%, with at least mild use disorder).

design_detail: Anonymous cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics), 2 to 26 October 2016, announced on the homepage of the American Kratom Association (AKA), which the author describes as an organization that favors kratom use and advocates for its continued legality, on its Facebook page, website forums and membership email list with weekly reminders, and shared on various other websites frequented by people who use kratom (speciosa.org and drugs-forum.com named as examples). Collection stopped once 10,000 responses were reached; the 8,049 completed responses (80.5%) were analysed. Single author; questionnaire built on variables of the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, covering demographics, health status, kratom use (reasons, self-reported amount per dose and doses per week, preparation, checklists of perceived beneficial and negative effects, negative effects when kratom was not taken for 12 to 48 hours with a severity rating, ever needing treatment because of kratom) and opinions on regulation. Analysis: frequencies, chi-square goodness-of-fit tests against equal category counts, and binomial logistic regressions of four reasons for use on demographics and of each perceived benefit and negative effect on amount per dose and doses per week. Read as the accepted manuscript.
can_establish: What 8,049 self-selected adults reached mainly through a kratom advocacy organization's online channels in October 2016 reported about themselves, their reasons for using kratom, the benefits and negative effects they perceived, negative effects when they went without kratom and any need for treatment, and how these reports varied with self-reported amount per dose and frequency of use.
cannot_establish: How common kratom use, its perceived benefits or its harms are among people in the US who use or have used kratom (no sampling frame; recruitment through an advocacy organization; people who stopped after harm, and anyone who died, are absent); whether kratom relieves pain, mood symptoms or opioid withdrawal (perceived effects, no comparison, no verification); thresholds of amount or frequency for benefit or harm (cross-sectional associations against the largest categories); or the frequency of withdrawal in the whole sample (reported only for respondents who reported a negative effect).

sample.recruitment: Online advertisement: the AKA homepage, Facebook page, website forums and membership email distribution with weekly reminders until 10,000 responses, plus information shared on various other websites frequented by people who use kratom, speciosa.org and drugs-forum.com named as examples; no incentive; IP addresses used, without being stored, to block repeat responses from one device (PDF p. 6, 2.1). The acknowledgment thanks the AKA for distributing the survey and assisting in collecting responses (PDF p. 14).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents acknowledged being 18 or older and taking part voluntarily; the survey was addressed to people currently using kratom, by self-declaration; only completed responses were analysed (8,049 of 10,000, 80.5%) (PDF p. 6). No other criteria.
sample.demographics: 56.91% men; age 18–20 2.63%, 21–30 25.32%, 31–40 34.64%, 41–50 20.45%, 51–60 12%, 61 or older 4.86%; non-Hispanic White 89.39%, Hispanic or Latino 3.42%, Black 0.76%; married 45.21%; employed for wages 56.83%, self-employed 15.03%, unable to work 8.49%; private insurance through an employer 47.31%, no insurance 14.09%, Medicaid 8.08%, Medicare 7.7%; household income $75,000 or more 28.67%, under $20,000 11.73%; at least some college 82.32% (PDF p. 8; Table 1, PDF pp. 18–19).
sample.attrition: 1,951 of the 10,000 responses (19.5%) were incomplete and excluded (editors' calculation). Item denominators then fall from 8,049 to between 6,981 and 7,893 without explanation.
sample.selection_effects: A volunteer sample reached through an advocacy organization that also assisted in collecting responses, and through other websites frequented by people who use kratom: people with good experiences and continuing use are likely over-represented, and people who stopped because of harm, and anyone who died, are absent. The author notes the AKA's advocacy, that online recruitment may skew toward younger and more affluent respondents, and that multiple responses from different devices could not be excluded (PDF pp. 6, 13).

exposure.measurement: Self-report only; neither kratom use nor the product was verified (PDF pp. 6–7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, in categories (as study conditions): amount per dose less than 1 g 504, 1–3 g 3,094, 3–5 g 2,487, 5–8 g 1,160, more than 8 g 360; doses per week 1–7: 2,607, 8–14: 2,162, 15–21: 1,834, 22–28: 554, 29–36: 295, 37–48: 76, more than 48: 77 (Tables 4 and 5, PDF pp. 24–25). Usual preparation (Table 2, headed N=8,069, PDF p. 21; each named form is taken by mouth, and the other forms are not specified): powder with a beverage 48.59%, powder pure or in pills 32.64%, self-prepared tea 13%, with food 2.19%, store-bought liquid shot 0.52%, other 3.07%. Time since first use (n=7,893): under 6 months 14.79%, 6 months to 1 year 18.89%, 1–2 years 28.01%, 2–5 years 28.58%, over 5 years 9.73% (Table 1, PDF p. 19).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking, alcohol and caffeine use were asked (PDF p. 7) but are not reported. Other drug use appears only through the reasons for use (illicit-drug or prescription-medicine dependency). Not controlled in any analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; respondents were addressed as people currently using kratom, by self-declaration.

comparison.controls: None. Within-sample logistic regressions compare demographic levels with reference levels (Table 3), and amount and frequency categories with the largest categories, more than 8 g per dose (n=360) and more than 48 doses per week (n=77) (Tables 4 and 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Health conditions, pain and opioid use before kratom use; severity of any opioid or other substance use disorder; product type and strength. The questionnaire asked about the length of the medical condition before kratom use and about treatment for substance use disorder (PDF p. 7), but neither is reported.

outcomes.instruments: A questionnaire designed for the study on BRFSS variables (in the supplementary material, not available for this card): yes or no items for four reasons for use; checklists of 9 perceived beneficial and 12 negative effects; an item on negative effects when kratom was not taken for more than 12, 24 or 48 hours, with severity rated from 1 (very severe) to 5 (not severe at all); and the question whether the respondent had ever needed medical or mental health care because of kratom use (PDF pp. 7–8; Tables 1, 3, 4 and 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation or piloting is reported, and no standard withdrawal or dependence instrument was used.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit and harm are what respondents ticked on the checklists; withdrawal-type effects are negative effects reported when kratom was not taken for 12 to 48 hours; toxicity requiring treatment is the self-reported lifetime need for medical or mental health care because of kratom use (PDF pp. 8, 11).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 25 outcomes (4 reasons, 9 benefits, 12 negative effects) were each modelled on predictors, giving 354 odds ratios in Tables 3 to 5 (editors' count: 36 demographic levels for each of 4 reasons, and 10 amount or frequency levels for each of 21 effects), plus 14 chi-square goodness-of-fit tests in Table 1.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages: reasons for use, pain 68% (4,811 of 7,060) and emotional or mental conditions 66.5% (4,684 of 7,047); prescription-medicine dependency 1,813 of 6,981 (26.0%) and illicit-drug dependency 539 of 7,029 (7.7%) (editors' calculations for the last two). Discussed kratom with a healthcare provider 40.05%. Perceived benefits: decreased pain 85.01%, increased energy 83.75%, less depressive mood 80.00%, reduced or stopped opioid painkillers 3,715 of 7,605 (48.8%, editors' calculation). Any negative effect 20.93% (1,652 of 7,893): nausea 12.75%, constipation 9.17%, dizziness or drowsiness 4.81%. Ever needed treatment because of kratom 0.65% (51 of 7,893). Negative effects when kratom was not taken: 703 of the 1,652 reporting any negative effect (42.55%; 8.9% of 7,893, editors' calculation), rated 1 or 2 on the 1 (very severe) to 5 scale by 351 of 703 (49.9%, editors' calculation). Odds ratios (95% CI) against more than 8 g per dose: nausea 0.23 (0.15–0.35) for less than 1 g to 0.58 (0.43–0.77) for 5–8 g; decreased pain 1.12 to 1.25, all intervals including 1 (Tables 4 and 5). No interval is given for any percentage; editors' calculation, Wilson 95% intervals: 0.65% (0.5% to 0.8%); 8.9% (8.3% to 9.6%).
analysis.covariates: Table 3 models: age, gender, marital status, race, employment, insurance, education and income together; Tables 4 and 5: amount per dose and doses per week (the Methods say all pertinent independent variables were entered in the same model, PDF pp. 7–8). No adjustment for health status, pain, duration of use or other substance use.
analysis.selective_reporting: Health-status items (weight, height, self-rated health, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, reasons for provider visits, pain level, diagnosed conditions), the length of the condition before kratom use, treatment for substance use disorder, change in condition with kratom, and the regulation opinions are listed among the survey items (PDF p. 7) but not reported. The shares answering yes to the two dependency reasons are not given in the text, only the counts in the Table 3 header. The withdrawal-type effects appear in neither the abstract nor the Highlights.
analysis.power: The Methods report a post-survey calculation of at least 85% power and 93% confidence for all models without saying for which effect size (PDF pp. 7–8). Rare outcomes (11 to 54 cases for fainting, shortness of breath, high blood pressure, diarrhoea and rapid heartbeat) and reference groups of 360 and 77 make many odds ratios unstable, with intervals up to 0.00–11467.11.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8,049 self-selected adults reached mainly through the AKA's online channels in October 2016, mostly White, employed and middle-aged, kratom was reported mainly for pain (68%) and emotional or mental conditions (66.5%), and 1,813 respondents gave a prescription-medicine dependency as a reason. Perceived benefits were common (decreased pain 85.01%); 20.93% reported negative effects, mostly nausea and constipation; 51 of 7,893 (0.65%) said they had ever needed treatment because of kratom; and 703 reported negative effects when they went 12 to 48 hours without kratom, half of them choosing one of the two most severe ratings (editors' calculation). Respondents reporting smaller amounts per dose less often reported most negative effects and some benefits, but decreased pain showed no association with amount or frequency.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that kratom shows a "dose-dependent opioid-like effect" providing perceived benefits in alleviating pain and mood disorders (PDF p. 3), but the Results found no dose-dependent effect for decreased pain (PDF p. 10). The Highlights call the 0.65% an incidence of kratom-related toxicity requiring treatment (PDF p. 3): it is a lifetime self-report by people still using kratom and recruited through an advocacy organization, so people who stopped after harm, and anyone who died, are missing, and the figure is not an incidence. The Discussion says the results further support kratom use for acute and chronic pain and strengthen the proposed mechanism for its analgesic effects (PDF pp. 11–12); perceived effects in a self-selected cross-sectional sample can support neither efficacy nor mechanism. The abstract places negative effects mainly at 5 g or more per dose and 22 or more doses per week (PDF p. 3), and the Results and Discussion name a threshold amount for perceived reduction of opioid painkillers and an amount and frequency sufficient for benefit (PDF pp. 10, 12); cross-sectional comparisons against the largest category cannot establish such thresholds, and in Table 5 the 5–8 g category still had lower odds of nausea, vomiting, constipation and dizziness or drowsiness than more than 8 g (PDF pp. 25–26). The Highlights and the abstract's Conclusions name opioid-related withdrawal symptoms, with pain and mood, among the main reasons for use (PDF pp. 3–4), but the closest items in Table 3 were answered yes far less often: a prescription-medicine dependency by 1,813 of 6,981 (26.0%) and an illicit-drug dependency by 539 of 7,029 (7.7%), against 68% for pain and 66.5% for mood (PDF p. 22; editors' calculations). The negative effects on going without kratom, reported by 703 respondents, are absent from the abstract and the Highlights, although the Discussion says they may indicate physical dependence (PDF p. 12). On the other side, the paper states the selection bias of online recruitment and the AKA's advocacy role (PDF pp. 6, 13) and asks for cautious interpretation (PDF p. 13). A headline version (kratom is safe, 0.65% harmed; kratom works for pain) would overstate it in both respects.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: of the later work, only Garcia-Romeu et al. (2020) was read for this card. Both surveys describe a middle-aged, mostly White, employed sample using kratom mainly for pain and mood, with very few reporting treatment for harms; both recruited heavily through the AKA and other websites frequented by people who use kratom, so their agreement does not show that the profile holds for people who use kratom generally. The project's Kratom list notes that there is no satisfactory prevalence estimate and that NSDUH kratom items from 2021 onward are the best available (Kratom list, Known gaps).

funding.funder: None: the research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (PDF p. 14).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state no conflict of interest (PDF p. 14; single author).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, College of Pharmacy, Department of Medicinal Chemistry, University of Florida. The AKA did not contribute financially to the design or conduct of the survey (PDF p. 13) but distributed it and assisted in collecting responses (acknowledgment, PDF p. 14); CDC and Dr Andrew Kruegel of Columbia University commented on the design and results (PDF p. 14). what_would_settle_it: A probability-based survey of US adults (or of a defined frame such as all purchasers) asking everyone validated questions on withdrawal, dependence and harms, followed by a prospective cohort of people starting kratom with verified use and product testing; for claimed benefits in pain, mood or opioid withdrawal, controlled trials.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The target is people in the US who use kratom; the frame is visitors, members and followers of an advocacy organization's website, forums, Facebook page and email list, plus other websites frequented by people who use kratom (two named as examples).

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: Self-selected volunteers; collection stopped at a fixed number of responses.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 8,049 completed responses give intervals of about ±1 percentage point for shares near 50% (editors' calculation); rare outcomes and the reference groups of 360 and 77 are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics, insurance, income and education are tabulated (Table 1), but the health-status, substance-use and treatment items that were collected are not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Only completed responses (80.5%) were analysed, and item denominators vary from 6,981 to 8,069 without explanation.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Unvalidated self-report checklists; no standard withdrawal or dependence measure; the withdrawal item counts only respondents who reported a negative effect; the treatment item is lifetime and does not separate outpatient care from hospitalization.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same online questionnaire for all respondents, but the item on negative effects when kratom was not taken was answered only by the 1,652 who reported a negative effect (its four answers sum to 1,652; Table 1, PDF p. 19), so withdrawal-type effects were not measured across all respondents.

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis
domains.note: Percentages without intervals; chi-square goodness-of-fit tests against equal category counts, which test nothing of interest; 354 odds ratios without correction; sparse cells with intervals up to 11467.11; italics and text disagree with the intervals in places.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: How many people saw the announcements is unknown; 80.5% of those who started completed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence, because the paper reports how often characteristics, reasons, perceived benefits and harms occurred among respondents. Editors' summary: high risk of bias for any prevalence beyond this sample: no frame, recruitment through an advocacy organization that also assisted in collecting responses, self-report without validated instruments for withdrawal or harm, and an unknowable response rate. The direction of bias is predictable: benefits overstated and harms understated relative to everyone who uses or has used kratom. Citable for: what 8,049 respondents reached through these channels in October 2016 reported (demographics; reasons; perceived benefits and negative effects; 0.65% lifetime need for treatment; negative effects on going without kratom in 703; fewer negative effects reported with smaller self-reported amounts), labelled as a self-selected, advocacy-linked sample. Not citable for: population prevalence, efficacy for pain, mood or opioid withdrawal, an incidence of toxicity, or thresholds of amount or frequency.

key_findings.finding: Against respondents reporting more than 8 g per dose (n=360), those in smaller amount categories had lower odds of most negative effects: nausea OR 0.23 (95% CI 0.15–0.35) for less than 1 g, 0.35 (0.26–0.45) for 1–3 g, 0.5 (0.38–0.65) for 3–5 g and 0.58 (0.43–0.77) for 5–8 g; constipation 0.17 (0.10–0.30) to 0.59 (0.43–0.83); vomiting 0.12 (0.06–0.26) to 0.53 (0.35–0.78); dizziness or drowsiness 0.15 (0.08–0.30) to 0.51 (0.35–0.74). key_findings.finding: Against more than 48 doses per week (n=77), less frequent use went with lower odds of nausea (for example OR 0.46, 0.26–0.82, at 8–14 doses), vomiting and constipation, but for rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, fainting and high blood pressure the odds ratios were mostly above 1 with very wide intervals: rapid heartbeat 33.53 (1.22–921.44) at 37–48 doses; fainting intervals up to 0.00–11467.11.

design_detail: CDC surveillance report (MMWR Notes from the Field, two pages) describing overdose deaths in which kratom was detected on postmortem toxicology, drawn from the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS). SUDORS abstracts, from death certificates and medical examiner or coroner reports including postmortem toxicology, unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths in which at least one opioid contributed, plus overdose deaths without a contributing opioid if a substance with opioid-like properties contributed (kratom is named as the only such substance); it records every substance detected, whether or not it contributed. 27 states: 11 for July 2016 to December 2017 and 16 only for July to December 2017; five states submitted a subset of counties covering at least 75% of their overdose deaths; data current as of 22 January 2019. Two overlapping groups are described: kratom-positive deaths (kratom detected on postmortem toxicology, n=152) and kratom-involved deaths (a medical examiner or coroner determined kratom to be a cause of death, n=91, all of them among the 152). Counts and percentages only; no rates, statistical tests or comparison with deaths in which kratom was not detected.
can_establish: How many overdose deaths entered into SUDORS in 27 states in 2016–2017 had kratom detected on postmortem toxicology, in how many of these a medical examiner or coroner named kratom as a cause of death, which other substances were named as causes in the same deaths, and which circumstances were recorded for these decedents.
cannot_establish: How many deaths kratom caused (involvement means a certifier listed it as a cause, almost always beside other drugs, by criteria the report does not give); how many overdose deaths had kratom present but undetected (testing was not documented and varied, and identification is method-dependent); kratom's share of all overdose deaths (SUDORS takes only deaths in which an opioid, or kratom, contributed); death rates among people who use kratom (no denominator of use); or whether the substances found differ from those in overdose deaths without kratom (no comparison group).

sample.recruitment: Registry. SUDORS is funded by CDC in 32 states and the District of Columbia; 27 states contributed deaths to this analysis (p. 326, text 2nd paragraph; footnotes † and ¶).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths in which at least one opioid contributed to death, and overdose deaths with no contributing opioid if kratom contributed (footnote §, p. 326). 11 states reported deaths for the whole period (Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, West Virginia, Wisconsin) and 16 only for July to December 2017 (footnote ¶). Florida, Illinois, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Washington submitted data for subsets of counties reflecting at least 75% of their overdose deaths (footnote †). No ICD codes are given in the report.
sample.demographics: Kratom-positive deaths: 116 men (76.3%) and 36 women (23.7%); non-Hispanic White 119 (91.5% of the 130 with race recorded), nonwhite 11 (8.5%); race and ethnicity missing for 22. Kratom-involved deaths: 69 men (75.8%), 22 women (24.2%); White 81 (93.1%); the nonwhite count is suppressed (fewer than 10). Age is not reported (Table, p. 327).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry counts). Race and ethnicity missing for 22 decedents (Table footnote †, p. 327).
sample.selection_effects: The denominator is SUDORS deaths, that is opioid-involved overdose deaths plus overdose deaths to which kratom contributed: an overdose death with kratom detected in which neither an opioid nor kratom was judged to contribute (for example a stimulant-only overdose) would not enter SUDORS (footnote §, p. 326). States contribute unequal periods (18 months for 11 states, 6 months for 16), and five contribute only some counties. Kratom can be found only where it was tested for, and the report says testing protocols were not documented and varied among and within states (p. 326, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Kratom-positive: kratom detected on postmortem toxicology; the specimen, analytical method, analyte and cut-off are not reported, and testing protocols were not documented and varied among and within states (p. 326, 3rd paragraph). Kratom-involved: a medical examiner or coroner determined kratom to be a cause of death; the criteria for that determination are not stated. Who decided: the medical examiner or coroner; CDC analysed the abstracted records.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; no postmortem concentrations, specimens or post-mortem intervals are reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the report. Other substances listed as a cause of death by the medical examiner or coroner are tabulated for both groups (fentanyl and analogues, heroin, benzodiazepines, prescription opioids, cocaine, alcohol, methamphetamine), and several could be listed for one death (Table, p. 327). Only 7 of the 91 kratom-involved decedents had kratom as the only substance testing positive, and the report says other substances cannot be ruled out for them (p. 326, 3rd paragraph). The Table gives substances named as causes, not all substances detected. Heroin was coded from heroin or 6-monoacetylmorphine (or morphine or codeine with evidence of heroin use), and fentanyl as a prescription opioid only when scene evidence pointed to prescription fentanyl (Table footnotes †† and §§; footnote **, p. 326).

comparison.controls: None. The two groups described overlap (the 91 kratom-involved deaths are part of the 152 kratom-positive deaths), and no figures are given for SUDORS deaths without kratom.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (registry counts). Circumstances (history of substance misuse, previous overdose, medically supervised pain treatment) come from death-investigation records and are given as evidence or no evidence, so no evidence does not mean the circumstance was absent.

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates and medical examiner or coroner reports, including postmortem toxicology results, abstracted into SUDORS (p. 326, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state that kratom identification is method-dependent, that the counts might therefore underestimate kratom-positive deaths to an extent that cannot be determined, and that documentation of postmortem toxicology testing protocols is needed (p. 327, text 5th and 6th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Kratom-positive: kratom detected on postmortem toxicology. Kratom-involved: kratom determined to be a cause of death by a medical examiner or coroner. Co-occurring substances: other substances listed as a cause of death. Circumstances: reported history of substance misuse (opioid or nonopioid), previous overdose reported, and evidence of current medically supervised pain treatment (Table, p. 327).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: counts and percentages only, with no statistical tests or confidence intervals.

analysis.effect_sizes: Kratom detected in 152 of 27,338 SUDORS overdose deaths (0.56%); named as a cause by a medical examiner or coroner in 91 of the 152 (59.9%), 7 of them with kratom the only substance testing positive (p. 326). Substances named as a cause, kratom-positive (n=152) and kratom-involved (n=91): any fentanyl 99 (65.1%) and 51 (56.0%); heroin 50 (32.9%) and 23 (25.3%); benzodiazepines 34 (22.4%) and 24 (26.4%); prescription opioids 30 (19.7%) and 22 (24.2%); cocaine 28 (18.4%) and 15 (16.5%); alcohol 19 (12.5%) and 11 (12.1%); methamphetamine 13 (8.6%) and not shown (a dash). History of substance misuse 123 (80.9%) and 71 (78.0%); no evidence of current medically supervised pain treatment 138 (90.8%) and 80 (87.9%); previous overdose reported 13 (8.5%) and 10 (11.0%) (Table, p. 327). Editors' calculation: at least one other substance tested positive in 84 of the 91 kratom-involved deaths (92.3%); 61 kratom-positive deaths had kratom detected but not named as a cause.
analysis.selective_reporting: Age, intent (unintentional or undetermined), the specimen tested, postmortem kratom concentrations, the share of the 27,338 deaths tested for kratom, and all substances detected (as against those named as causes) are not reported. The 61 kratom-positive deaths in which kratom was not named as a cause are not described separately.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive counts). Subsets are small: 7 deaths with kratom as the only substance detected; cells under 10 are suppressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Kratom was detected in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths entered into SUDORS from 27 states in July 2016 to December 2017 (0.56%). Medical examiners or coroners named it as a cause in 91; in 84 of these at least one other substance tested positive (editors' calculation), fentanyl was named as a cause in 51 (56.0%), and 7 had kratom as the only substance detected, with testing for other substances undocumented. About 80% of decedents had a recorded history of substance misuse and about 90% no evidence of current supervised pain treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report is cautious: it keeps the words kratom-positive and kratom-involved throughout, says testing protocols were not documented and varied, that identification is method-dependent and the counts may be underestimates, and concludes that kratom was present mainly in deaths from overdoses related to substance misuse and usually with several other substances (pp. 326–327). Two statements go beyond what is shown: the text cites the Table for multiple substances detected in almost all decedents, but the Table lists only substances named as causes (p. 326, 4th paragraph; Table, p. 327); and kratom-involved can be read as caused by kratom, although the certifiers' criteria are not given and other drugs were named as causes in most of these deaths. A headline version would overstate in either direction: a count of 91 kratom deaths turns a certifier's listing amid polysubstance deaths into deaths caused by kratom, and fewer than 1% of overdoses ignores that kratom was not routinely or documentably tested for and that SUDORS selects deaths in which an opioid contributed.

timeline.event: Anwar, Law and Schier (2016), MMWR: kratom exposures reported to US poison centers 2010–2015, described in Grundmann (2017) as 660 calls, 49 (7.4%) classified as major (Grundmann 2017, PDF p. 4); not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: only this report was read for this card. It is a national-scale CDC count of overdose deaths with kratom detected and of those in which certifiers named kratom as a cause, and it is the source of the widely repeated figure of 91 kratom-involved deaths. Its own caveats (undocumented, varying toxicology; method-dependent identification) and the near-universal presence of other drugs mean it cannot settle how many deaths kratom causes. The project's Kratom list places the forensic-toxicology critiques (Papsun 2019 and 2023), later case series (Schmitt 2021, Eccarius 2026) and the later CDC SUDORS analyses (report R4) on the reading list for that question.

funding.funder: CDC: the authors are CDC staff (Division of Unintentional Injury Prevention, National Center for Injury Prevention and Control), and SUDORS is CDC-funded (pp. 326–327). No separate funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed and submitted the ICMJE form for disclosure of potential conflicts of interest; no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed (p. 327).
funding.affiliations_note: Government surveillance report. The acknowledgment thanks the participating state agencies (health departments, vital registrar offices, coroner and medical examiner offices) and Bruce Goldberger of the University of Florida College of Medicine (p. 327).

what_would_settle_it: Standardized postmortem testing for mitragynine and other kratom alkaloids in all suspected overdose deaths, with documented specimens, panels and concentrations, explicit criteria for naming kratom as a cause, the same testing in deaths from other causes, and linkage to population estimates of kratom use, so that the share of deaths with kratom present, the contribution of co-detected drugs and rates among people who use kratom could be estimated.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: All deaths entered into SUDORS in the period; no sampling.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 27,338 deaths and 152 kratom-positive deaths; the kratom-only subset (7) and suppressed cells are too small to describe.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: States, periods and inclusion rules are given in footnotes, and sex, race and circumstances in the Table; age, intent, specimens and toxicology panels are not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Every kratom-positive death is described; race and ethnicity are missing for 22 of 152.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Kratom detection depends on testing that was not documented and varied among and within states, so the denominator mixes deaths tested and not tested for kratom; the criteria for naming kratom as a cause are not given.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Testing protocols varied among and within states (p. 326), and identification is method-dependent (p. 327).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths with a substance detected in a surveillance register (round brief; earlier SUDORS cards). The counts are transparent and internally consistent, but the measurement that defines the main figures is not standard: whether kratom was tested for, by what method and in which specimen varied and was not documented, and the criteria for naming kratom as a cause are not stated. Editors' summary: high risk of bias for any estimate of how often kratom is present in, or contributes to, overdose deaths; the direction is mainly toward undercounting presence (as the authors say), while attribution as a cause may be over-read because other drugs were named in most of these deaths. Citable for: in SUDORS deaths from 27 states in July 2016 to December 2017, kratom was detected in 152 of 27,338 (0.56%), certifiers named it as a cause in 91, 7 of these had kratom as the only substance detected, fentanyl was named as a cause in 65.1% of kratom-positive and 56.0% of kratom-involved deaths, and about 80% of decedents had a recorded history of substance misuse. Not citable for: deaths caused by kratom alone, kratom's share of all overdose deaths, rates among people who use kratom, or trends.

key_findings.finding: Of 27,338 overdose deaths in July 2016 to December 2017 entered into SUDORS from 27 states, 152 (0.56%) tested positive for kratom on postmortem toxicology; testing protocols were not documented and varied among and within states.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: The PDF's embedded document summary (file properties) gives 27,340 deaths; the printed text, checked on the rendered page, gives 27,338. 152 of either rounds to 0.56%.

key_findings.finding: A medical examiner or coroner determined kratom to be a cause of death (kratom-involved) for 91 of the 152 kratom-positive decedents (59.9%); for 7 of these 91, kratom was the only substance that tested positive, and the report adds that the presence of other substances cannot be ruled out for them.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: at least one other substance tested positive in 84 of the 91 kratom-involved deaths (92.3%). The criteria for naming kratom as a cause are not given.

key_findings.finding: Other substances listed as a cause of death, kratom-positive (n=152) and kratom-involved (n=91) decedents: any fentanyl including analogues 99 (65.1%) and 51 (56.0%); heroin 50 (32.9%) and 23 (25.3%); benzodiazepines 34 (22.4%) and 24 (26.4%); prescription opioids 30 (19.7%) and 22 (24.2%); cocaine 28 (18.4%) and 15 (16.5%); alcohol 19 (12.5%) and 11 (12.1%); methamphetamine 13 (8.6%) and not shown. More than one substance could be listed per death.
key_findings.locator: Text, 4th paragraph (p. 326, right column); Table, co-occurring substances rows and footnote ** (p. 327)
key_findings.note: The methamphetamine cell for kratom-involved deaths is a dash without a footnote mark; the suppression footnote (fewer than 10 deaths) is attached only to the nonwhite cell, so the dash is probably, but not explicitly, a suppressed count. The prescription-opioid row is a coded class of substances (oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, buprenorphine and others; Table footnote §§), and the analysis does not distinguish drugs prescribed to the decedent from diverted ones (footnote **, p. 326; Table footnote §§, p. 327).

key_findings.finding: Recorded circumstances, kratom-positive and kratom-involved decedents: evidence of a history of substance misuse (opioid or nonopioid) 123 (80.9%) and 71 (78.0%); no evidence of current medically supervised pain treatment 138 (90.8%) and 80 (87.9%); one or more previous overdoses reported 13 (8.5%) and 10 (11.0%).
key_findings.locator: Text, 4th paragraph (p. 326); Table, circumstance rows (p. 327)
key_findings.note: These are recorded as evidence or no evidence in investigation records; no evidence is not the same as absence.

key_findings.finding: Decedents: kratom-positive 116 men (76.3%) and 36 women (23.7%), non-Hispanic White 119 (91.5%) and nonwhite 11 (8.5%) of those with race recorded (race missing for 22); kratom-involved 69 men (75.8%), 22 women (24.2%), White 81 (93.1%). Age is not reported.
key_findings.locator: Table, sex and race rows and footnotes † and §

key_findings.finding: SUDORS takes unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths in which at least one opioid contributed, plus overdoses without a contributing opioid if kratom contributed, and records all substances detected whether or not they contributed. 11 states reported for July 2016 to December 2017 and 16 only for July to December 2017; five states submitted subsets of counties reflecting at least 75% of their overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: Text, 2nd paragraph; footnotes †, § and ¶

key_findings.finding: The authors state that kratom-positive deaths were under 1% of all SUDORS overdose deaths, that kratom identification is method-dependent so the data might underestimate kratom-positive deaths to an extent that cannot be determined, that kratom was present mainly in deaths from overdoses related to substance misuse and most often with multiple other substances, and that documentation of testing protocols is needed to clarify how far kratom contributes to fatal overdoses.
key_findings.locator: Text, 5th and 6th paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Context given by the report: the national poison center database documented 1,807 calls about kratom exposure in 2011–2017 (cited from Post et al., 2019); FDA issued a public health advisory in November 2017; kratom was not a scheduled controlled substance as of April 2019.
key_findings.locator: Text, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures cited by the report, not its own data.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Table, one or more previous overdoses is 13 (8.5%) and none 139 (91.5%) of 152, while the same 13 of 152 is printed as 8.6% in the methamphetamine row; editors' calculation: 13 of 152 is 8.6% and 139 of 152 is 91.4%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding slip; cite the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites the Table for multiple substances detected in almost all decedents, but the Table lists only substances named as a cause of death, not all substances detected; the only count of single-substance deaths is the 7 among the 91 kratom-involved decedents, and the kratom-positive deaths in which kratom was not named as a cause are not described (editors' calculation: 61 deaths, 152 minus 91).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot be quantified for the 152; claims should use 84 of 91 kratom-involved deaths with at least one other substance detected, and say that testing for other substances was not documented.
